content: The monkeypox virus, also referred to as MPXV, was first identified in 1958 in monkeys that were transported from Singapore to Denmark. The first human case of monkeypox was reported in 1970 in the Republic of the Congo. The virus belongs to the Orthopoxvirus genus within the Poxviridae family. It is capable of being transmitted through animal-to-animal, animal-to-human, and human-to-human contact. Evidence for mother-to-child transmission is limited. Historically, monkeypox was first identified in monkeys in 1958, and the first human case was documented in a hospitalized child in the Republic of the Congo in 1970. Over the following decades, cases were reported in 11 African countries, with more than 400 cases recorded by the late 1980s. In the early 1990s, the number of cases declined significantly, with no cases reported between 1993 and 1995. However, in 1996, an outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo led to a large number of suspected cases, though only a small number were laboratory-confirmed. In 2003, 47 confirmed and probable cases were reported in the United States. In subsequent years, cases were periodically recorded in non-endemic regions, such as the United Kingdom and Singapore, all of which were linked to travel from endemic areas. In May 2022, clusters of monkeypox cases were identified globally, with 109 confirmed cases and 87 suspected cases reported by May 22, 2022. By June 2, 2022, 780 cases were reported to the World Health Organization (WHO), and by June 15, 2022, 2,103 laboratory-confirmed cases, including one death, were documented. The monkeypox virus is a member of the Orthopoxvirus genus and has a linear double-stranded DNA genome that replicates in the cytoplasm of infected cells. There are two genetic clades of the virus: the West African clade and the Central African (Congo Basin) clade. Transmission can occur through direct contact with body fluids, lesions, or respiratory secretions of an infected person or animal, as well as through contact with contaminated materials such as clothing or bedding. The role of vaginal fluids and semen in transmission is still under investigation. Animal-to-human transmission can occur through invasive bites or scratches that break the skin, as well as direct contact with lesions or bodily fluids of infected animals. Human-to-human transmission occurs through close physical contact, direct contact with lesions or bodily fluids, respiratory secretions, contaminated materials, or via the placenta from mother to fetus. The differential diagnosis for monkeypox includes smallpox, chickenpox, scabies, syphilis, bacterial skin infections, and drug-associated allergies. The precise prevalence and incidence of monkeypox are difficult to determine due to underreporting in past outbreaks. In the 1970s and 1980s, the median age of infection was 4 to 5 years. By the 2000s and 2010s, the median age increased to 10 to 21 years. In May 2022, the average median age of infection was 37 years. Monkeypox is typically a self-limiting disease, with symptoms resolving within 2 to 4 weeks. Complications are rare but may include secondary bacterial infections such as pneumonia, sepsis, encephalitis, corneal inflammation, and conjunctivitis. Key historical and symptomatic information for diagnosis includes recent travel to endemic areas or contact with infected individuals, animals, or contaminated materials. Initial symptoms include fever, chills, lymphadenopathy, headache, myalgia, followed by a skin rash with multiple lesions that evolve simultaneously. The progression of lesions includes macular (1–2 days), papular (1–2 days), vesicular (1–2 days), pustular (5–7 days), and scab stages (7–14 days). Physical examination findings depend on the stage of the disease and may include low-grade fever, enlarged lymph nodes (submental, submandibular, cervical, inguinal), and a skin rash with the characteristic progression of lesions. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is the preferred diagnostic test for monkeypox due to its sensitivity and accuracy. Samples should be obtained from skin lesions, specifically the roof or fluid from vesicles and pustules, as well as dry crusts. PCR blood tests are usually inconclusive because the virus does not persist long in the blood. There are no electrocardiogram (EKG) findings associated with monkeypox. Ultrasound may be useful for assessing fetal well-being in pregnant women with laboratory-confirmed monkeypox. Currently, there is no proven, safe treatment for monkeypox. To contain outbreaks, the CDC recommends the use of smallpox vaccines, cidofovir, ST-246, and vaccinia immune globulin. Vaccines are not currently available to the public, but in the event of a larger outbreak, the CDC will establish guidelines for vaccine distribution. Surgery is not indicated for monkeypox, as it is generally a self-limiting disease with symptoms lasting 2 to 4 weeks. Primary prevention measures include pre-exposure prophylaxis with ACAM2000 or JYNNEOS vaccines for individuals at risk of exposure based on occupational assessments. The CDC recommends proper hand hygiene with soap and water or alcohol-based hand sanitizers after contact with infected animals or humans. Close contact with lesions, bodily fluids, respiratory droplets, or contaminated materials such as bedding or towels should be avoided. Personal protective equipment (PPE) is essential for healthcare workers handling patients. Infected patients should be isolated to reduce the spread of the virus.
